clue.text: Rayner announced? Hiding in kitchen, I'm busy!

definitions.note: said aloud, Rayner sounds like 'rainer', something that brings rain, which is a rain cloud

indicators.note: hiding in says the answer sits concealed inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Food critic Jay Rayner calls from the kitchen that he is too busy.
explanation.walkthrough: Jay Rayner is a British food critic; the definition works only by sound, as 'rainer'. The answer runs through kitcheN IM BUSy.
explanation.definitionFit: A nimbus is a grey rain-bearing cloud, so it is literally a 'rainer', the punning sense of the critic's surname.

clue.text: National PM once doffing cap

indicators.note: doffing his cap means the former prime minister loses his head, his first letter

parts.note: Benjamin Disraeli was a 19th-century British prime minister

explanation.surface: A former prime minister raises his hat in a show of patriotism.
explanation.definitionFit: A national is a citizen of a country, here a citizen of Israel.

clue.text: Shout about right for noisy fight

indicators.note: about says the word for shout is placed around the letter for right

parts.note: to bawl is to shout loudly

explanation.surface: Someone yells about being in the right, which turns into a loud fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A brawl is a rough, rowdy scuffle, a fight with a lot of noise.

clue.text: All kicking off with simply incredible theatre, take a pew!

indicators.note: all kicking off asks for the opening letter of each of the next words

explanation.surface: At a wonderful play, everyone is told to settle into their seats as it begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take a pew' is a British idiom for sit down.
explanation.definitionFit: To take a pew is a jokey idiom for sitting down, a pew being a church bench.

clue.text: Hospital an intergovernmental minister runs — big headache!

parts.note: H is the map abbreviation for hospital
Michael Gove was the UK minister for Levelling Up, Housing, Communities and Intergovernmental Relations
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A minister rushes around a hospital, giving everyone a headache.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangover is the morning-after sickness from drinking, typically including a pounding head.

clue.text: One keeps everything: more difficult keeping nothing

indicators.note: keeping says the word for more difficult holds the zero inside it

parts.note: harder means more difficult
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Holding on to everything you own only makes life harder.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarder is a person who stockpiles and refuses to throw things away.

clue.text: Far from urban, alfresco event ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately asks for the final letter of each of the three words before it

explanation.surface: An open-air event a long way from the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Far from works as a negative, as in 'far from happy' meaning not happy.

clue.text: Fruit, lemon gone wrong

indicators.note: gone wrong suggests letters that have been scrambled; 'wrong' rearranges the two words before it

explanation.surface: A piece of fruit, a lemon, has gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone' is part of the fodder, not of the indicator: only 'wrong' signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogen melon is a variety of small, sweet cantaloupe-type melon, developed in Israel.

clue.text: Land observed climbing in Dubai, not sea

indicators.note: climbing says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the answer lies inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A traveller in Dubai notices the land rather than the water.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft gave the hidden word no indicator; 'in' is the word that signals it.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonia is a Baltic country, so it is a land, one the solver has 'observed' hidden in the clue.

clue.text: With jam finally going in, make a light meal

indicators.note: going in says that last letter is placed inside the other letters

parts.note: to create is to make

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of jam

explanation.surface: A recipe step: add the jam last when preparing a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: A cream tea is a British afternoon snack of scones with jam and clotted cream, served with tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A cream tea is a modest afternoon spread rather than a full meal, so it counts as a light one.

clue.text: Crime in newspaper?

parts.note: a crime, read as the name of the pink business paper this puzzle is printed in, with 'the' in front

explanation.surface: Crime stories in the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as THE FT, the answer is the Financial Times, the paper carrying this crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: Theft is the offence of stealing property, and respaced it names the Financial Times.

clue.text: Irishman making pictures put country on wiggly line

indicators.note: in an across clue, putting one thing on another places it after it
a wiggly line is bent out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: Jordan is a country in the Middle East

explanation.surface: An Irish artist paints a country's border as a squiggly line.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Jordan is an Irish film director, maker of The Crying Game, so he makes motion pictures.

clue.text: Opening bank vaults first of all, promissory notes plain to see

indicators.note: first of all takes the opening letter of each of the first three words

parts.note: IOUs are written promises to repay a debt

explanation.surface: Breaking into a bank's vault, the robbers find IOUs on open display.
explanation.definitionFit: Obvious means easily perceived or evident, so it can be clearly seen.

clue.text: Drink taken before match — something formal?

indicators.note: taken before places the drink word ahead of the match word in this down answer

parts.note: to neck is British slang for downing a drink quickly
a tie is a match, as in a cup tie

explanation.surface: A quick drink before the game, in a formal setting.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a cup tie is a knockout match, and to neck a drink is to gulp it.
explanation.definitionFit: A necktie is part of formal dress, worn with a suit; the question mark marks the example.

clue.text: Battle covered by Simon Schama

indicators.note: covered by says the answer is concealed within the name that follows

explanation.surface: A battle discussed by historian Simon Schama.
explanation.definitionFit: Mons in Belgium gave its name to a 1914 First World War battle.

clue.text: Journalist and broadcaster, fan of fruit?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., the BBC radio presenter and journalist
second meaning: read as ..., a person who loves figs

explanation.walkthrough: Fi Glover is a British radio presenter; split differently her name becomes someone keen on figs.
explanation.definitionFit: The name Fi Glover respaced gives fig lover, an admirer of a particular fruit.

clue.text: Absurd, ridiculous label inscribed with a word expressing revulsion

indicators.note: inscribed with says the shuffled letters have more written inside them
ridiculous suggests something knocked out of sense, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: ugh is an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: A silly label has a disgusted exclamation written on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ridiculous' shuffles the letters to LABLE, and 'inscribed with' writes the A and the exclamation in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something laughable is so ridiculous it deserves only mockery.

clue.text: Where wine found, someone flogging it to the speaker?

indicators.note: to the speaker says the word is heard rather than written

parts.note: flogging is British slang for selling, so one flogging it is a seller

explanation.surface: Asking where the wine is, and who is selling it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellar is an underground room where bottles of wine are stored.

clue.text: Counterfeit, native American money, reportedly?

indicators.note: reportedly says the phrase is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: the Sioux are a Native American people; dough is slang for money

explanation.surface: Fake currency passed off as Native American money.
explanation.definitionFit: Pseudo means sham or not genuine, much as counterfeit goods are imitations.

clue.text: Slight injustice originally inspiring an author from Morocco

parts.note: slight means slim or slender

indicators.note: originally picks the first letter of injustice
inspiring, like originally, points to how something starts, the very first letter that sets off the word injustice

explanation.surface: A small wrong sets a Moroccan writer off on a new book.
explanation.walkthrough: Leila Slimani is a French-Moroccan novelist and Prix Goncourt winner. The clue names the I before AN, but it goes in last; the wordplay is loose there.
explanation.definitionFit: Leila Slimani was born in Rabat, so she is a writer from Morocco.

clue.text: Set off from school in time

indicators.note: in says the school sits within the word for time

parts.note: a date is a point in time
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: Leaving school on time.
explanation.definitionFit: To detonate a bomb is to set it off, triggering the explosion.

clue.text: Alistair, sweetie!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Alistair ..., former UK Chancellor of the Exchequer
second meaning: a term of endearment

explanation.walkthrough: Alistair Darling was Chancellor of the Exchequer, Britain's finance minister, under Gordon Brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Darling serves both as the surname of a Labour Chancellor and as an affectionate address.

clue.text: Supportive structure in anagram of letters

indicators.note: anagram of says outright that the next word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A support frame is spelt out in a puzzle of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A trestle is a frame of a beam on splayed legs used to support a table top.

clue.text: Food served up, gorgeous thing

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ... of food brought to the table
second meaning: slang for an attractive person

explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' looks like a reversal signal, but nothing is reversed: it is part of the first meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a prepared course of food and, informally, a very good-looking person.

clue.text: Cachet in clubs rare by the way

indicators.note: by means beside, so the road sits next to the other letters

parts.note: a street is a way or road
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
rare meat is red inside

explanation.surface: At nightclubs, prestige is rare around here.
explanation.definitionFit: Street cred is credibility among young, fashionable people, a kind of social prestige.

clue.text: Vessel, one empty boat

parts.note: a can is a container, a vessel

indicators.note: empty removes the inside of the word one, leaving its outer letters

explanation.surface: One ship with nobody aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A canoe is a light narrow boat paddled by hand.

clue.text: Rudd with fishy bream?

definitions.note: Amber Rudd is a former UK Home Secretary, so the answer is the name that goes with Rudd

indicators.note: fishy hints at something suspect, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A rudd, a freshwater fish, sits next to a bream.
explanation.walkthrough: Rudd and bream are both freshwater fish, which hides that Rudd is the politician Amber Rudd.
explanation.definitionFit: Amber is the first name of the Conservative politician Amber Rudd.

clue.text: Josh, one of those in a cage

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to josh is to tease

definitions.text: one of those in a cage
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a bone of the ribcage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Josh' looks like a name but is a verb meaning tease.
explanation.definitionFit: Rib means to tease playfully and is also one of the curved bones forming the chest cage.

clue.text: I play with words, it's in my freedom to break rules

indicators.note: in says the wordplay sits inside the word my

parts.note: taken as written
a pun is wordplay
it, with 's read as 'is' linking it to what follows

explanation.surface: A punster claims it is their right to break the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Impunity is exemption from punishment, so you can break the rules without consequence.

clue.text: Bit short — not quite a birdie!

indicators.note: short means cut off at the end, dropping the last letter

parts.note: a part is a bit, a portion

explanation.surface: A golfer just misses a birdie.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf, par is the standard score for a hole, one stroke worse than a birdie.

clue.text: Potpourri, GBA?

parts.note: GBA is what you get when BAG is mixed, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A potpourri labelled with a curious set of initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixed bag is an assortment of varied things, just as a potpourri is a medley.

clue.text: Severe labouring for Shadow Chancellor

indicators.note: labouring suggests toiling and struggling, so the letters are worked into new order; Labour is also her party

explanation.surface: A harsh Labour figure takes on the shadow finance job.
explanation.definitionFit: Rachel Reeves was Labour's Shadow Chancellor, the opposition's finance spokesperson, before becoming Chancellor.
